title: Reaction Types and Rates
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Reaction Types and Rates Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Identify patterns in synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions and investigate the factors that affect reaction rates (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 10 science worksheets on chemical reactions: synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions, the reactivity series, collision theory, and how temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts affect reaction rate. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts change how often particles collide successfully.
body_html:
How to think about it

Many reactions follow simple patterns.

  • Synthesis: A + B → AB. Decomposition: AB → A + B. Displacement: A + BC → AC + B, when A is more reactive than B.
  • Collision theory: particles react when they collide with enough energy in the right direction.
  • Rate increases with higher temperature, higher concentration, larger surface area (smaller pieces) and a catalyst.
Example

Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Type?

zinc replaces copper

Answer: displacement

Example

Why does powder react faster than a lump?

more surface area

more collisions

Answer: larger surface area

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst is used up in the reaction.
  • Thinking a large lump reacts faster than powder.
  • Mixing up synthesis (joining) and decomposition (breaking down).

faq.q: How do I tell the reaction types apart?
faq.a: Synthesis has one product; decomposition has one reactant; displacement has an element swapping places with another element in a compound.
It says reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy and in the right orientation. Anything that increases successful collisions speeds up the reaction.
A catalyst gives the reaction an easier pathway that needs less energy, so more collisions succeed. It is not used up.

items.q: Butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: Will copper displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution?
c: No, copper is less reactive than zinc.
Yes, all metals displace each other.
items.e: Only a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

items.q: Which type of reaction is 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂?
items.e: One reactant breaks into two products.

items.q: Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: Which general pattern matches Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: This is displacement.

items.q: What does combustion always need?
items.e: Fuel + O₂.

items.q: Which general pattern matches C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: This is combustion.

items.q: In a decomposition reaction, what happens?
c: one compound breaks into simpler substances
items.e: AB → A + B.

items.q: Propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: In a synthesis reaction, what happens?
c: two or more substances combine into one
items.e: A + B → AB.

items.q: Why does sodium react violently with water but gold does not?
c: Sodium loses its 1 valence electron very easily.
items.e: Activity depends on outer electrons.

items.q: Which type of reaction is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO?
items.e: Two reactants make one product.

items.q: Pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: Which general pattern matches Fe + CuSO<sub>4</sub> → FeSO<sub>4</sub> + Cu?
items.e: This is displacement.

items.q: Octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: Why does increasing the concentration of an acid speed up its reaction with magnesium?
c: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so more collisions.
items.e: Rate depends on the frequency of successful collisions.

items.q: What is a displacement reaction?
c: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound
a compound breaks down by heating
items.e: Example: zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.

items.q: What are reactants?
c: the substances made by a reaction
the substances at the start of a reaction
items.e: Left side.

items.q: What is a synthesis reaction?
c: two or more substances combine to make one product (A + B → AB)
one substance breaks into two or more (AB → A + B)
a more reactive element swaps places with a less reactive one
items.e: Example: iron + sulfur → iron sulfide.

items.q: What are products?
c: the substances made by a reaction
items.e: Right side.

items.q: Using the reactivity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au), which metal is more reactive: lead or calcium?
items.e: Higher in the list = loses electrons more easily.

items.q: A piece of iron is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Will a displacement reaction occur? (Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au)
c: No. Metals never react with solutions.
No. Iron is less active than copper, so no reaction occurs.
Yes. Any metal replaces any other metal.
Yes. Iron is more active than copper, so it replaces it.
items.e: A metal replaces only metals below it in the reactivity series.

items.q: A piece of lead is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Will a displacement reaction occur? (Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au)
c: Yes. Any metal replaces any other metal.
No. Lead is less active than copper, so no reaction occurs.
No. Metals never react with solutions.
Yes. Lead is more active than copper, so it replaces it.
items.e: A metal replaces only metals below it in the reactivity series.

items.q: Magnesium reacts with nitrogen gas. What is the formula of the product?
items.e: Magnesium loses 2 electrons and nitrogen gains 3; the charges must cancel.

items.q: Using the reactivity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au), which metal is more reactive: copper or zinc?
items.e: Higher in the list = loses electrons more easily.

items.q: Which general pattern matches 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO?
items.e: This is synthesis.

items.q: Why does increasing the temperature speed up a reaction?
c: Particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy.
items.e: Food goes off faster on a hot day.

items.q: A piece of iron is placed in silver nitrate solution. Will a displacement reaction occur? (Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au)
c: No. Metals never react with solutions.
Yes. Iron is more active than silver, so it replaces it.
Yes. Any metal replaces any other metal.
No. Iron is less active than silver, so no reaction occurs.
items.e: A metal replaces only metals below it in the reactivity series.

items.q: Sugar dissolves in tea. What kind of change is this?
c: a physical change, because the substance stays the same
a chemical change, because new substances form
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: Bubbles form when bicarb soda is added to vinegar. What kind of change is this?
c: a physical change, because only the form changes
a chemical change, because new substances form
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: A match gives off light and heat. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because new substances form
a physical change, because only the form changes
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: Jack collects the gas from marble chips and acid every 30 s. The volume rises quickly then levels off. Why does it level off?
c: The gas stops being a gas.
One of the reactants has been used up.
items.e: The reaction has finished.

items.q: Calcium reacts with sulfur. What is the formula of the product?
items.e: Calcium loses 2 electrons and sulfur gains 2; the charges must cancel.

items.q: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?
c: They must be the same colour.
They must collide with enough energy and in the right orientation.
items.e: More successful collisions mean a faster rate.

items.q: Zara wants a fair test of how surface area affects rate. What should she keep the same?
c: the mass of marble, the volume and concentration of acid, and the temperature
the size of the marble pieces
items.e: Only the surface area should change.

items.q: Ella's graph shows two reactions. Line A is steeper at the start than line B. What does this mean?
c: Reaction A has a faster initial rate.
items.e: A steeper slope means a faster rate.

items.q: Does aluminium react with hydrochloric acid? (Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au)
c: No, it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
Only if the metal is melted.
items.e: Metals above hydrogen replace it from acids.

items.q: A clear solution turns cloudy and a yellow solid forms when two solutions mix. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because new substances form
a physical change, because only the form changes
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: Ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) burns completely in oxygen. What are the products?
items.e: Complete combustion of a compound of C and H (and O) gives CO₂ and H₂O.

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide fizzes and the container gets warm when yeast is added. What kind of change is this?
c: a physical change, because only the form changes
a chemical change, because new substances form
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: Use collision theory. Why does increasing the surface area speed up a reaction?
c: More particles are exposed, so collisions are more frequent.
The particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy.
There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent.
items.e: Rate depends on how often particles collide with enough energy.

items.q: What is a decomposition reaction?
c: two substances join to make one
an element swaps places in a compound
one substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances
an acid reacts with a base
items.e: Example: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide.

items.q: Use collision theory. Why does increasing the pressure of a gas speed up a reaction?
c: There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy.
The particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent.
More particles are exposed, so collisions are more frequent.
items.e: Rate depends on how often particles collide with enough energy.

items.q: How does increasing concentration affect the rate?
c: It increases the rate because collisions are more frequent.
items.e: More particles per volume.

items.q: One large lump of zinc is used instead of zinc granules. Which explains the change in rate?
c: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.
Less surface area means fewer collisions.
More particles in the same volume collide more often.
Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: The magnesium-acid experiment is repeated using half the mass of magnesium ribbon. How does the total volume of hydrogen collected change?
items.e: The acid is in excess, so the magnesium limits the amount of hydrogen.

items.q: What is a reaction rate?
c: how much product is made in total
how fast reactants are used up or products are made
items.e: Change per unit time.

items.q: The hydrogen peroxide experiment is repeated using half the volume of the same hydrogen peroxide solution. How does the total volume of oxygen collected change?
items.e: There is half as much hydrogen peroxide to decompose.

items.q: Which change speeds up a reaction for this reason? “There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent.”
c: increasing the pressure of a gas
items.e: Match the change to its explanation.

items.q: A more concentrated acid is used. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: More particles in the same volume collide more often.

items.q: The acid is cooled in an ice bath. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.

items.q: The acid is heated from 20 °C to 40 °C. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Lower temperature and no light slow its decomposition.
Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
More particles in the same volume collide more often.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: Enzymes in saliva are added to starch. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Enzymes are biological catalysts.

items.q: A reaction finishes in 30 s at one temperature and 60 s at another. Which run was faster?
items.e: Less time = faster.

items.q: Which change speeds up a reaction for this reason? “The particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent.”
c: increasing the pressure of a gas
items.e: Match the change to its explanation.

items.q: The marble chip experiment is repeated using a more dilute acid (still in excess). How does the total volume of carbon dioxide collected change?
items.e: There are fewer acid particles per unit volume, so collisions are less frequent.

items.q: Does a catalyst change how much product forms?
c: No. It only makes the reaction reach the end sooner.
items.e: Same yield, faster.

items.q: The magnesium-acid experiment is repeated using twice the mass of magnesium ribbon (acid still in excess). How does the total volume of hydrogen collected change?
items.e: More magnesium gives more hydrogen in total.

items.q: Which change speeds up a reaction for this reason? “Particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy.”
c: increasing the pressure of a gas
items.e: Match the change to its explanation.

items.q: Marble chips are crushed into powder. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.

items.q: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The graph shows the volume of hydrogen collected. What is the total volume of hydrogen made?
items.e: The graph levels off at 80 cm³ when the magnesium is used up.

items.q: A flask on a balance loses 0.2 g of gas in 10 s (Mei's experiment). What is the average rate of mass loss?
Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The graph shows the volume of hydrogen collected. About how long does it take to collect half of the total volume of hydrogen?
items.e: Half of 48 cm³ is 24 cm³; read across to the curve and down to the time axis.

items.q: Tom collects 100 mL of carbon dioxide in 40 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
Why does powdered marble react faster with acid than a single marble chip of the same mass?
c: The powder has a larger surface area for collisions.
items.e: Grain dust explosions in silos happen for this reason.

items.q: Priya collects 100 mL of carbon dioxide in 50 s. What is the average rate of gas production?
Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The graph shows the volume of hydrogen collected. About how long does it take to collect half of the total volume of hydrogen?
items.e: Half of 60 cm³ is 30 cm³; read across to the curve and down to the time axis.

items.q: Why are enzymes important in living things?
c: They are biological catalysts that speed up reactions in cells.
They are used up in reactions.
items.e: Digestive enzymes break down food.

items.q: A flask on a balance loses 0.1 g of gas in 10 s (Kai's experiment). What is the average rate of mass loss?
What does a catalyst do?
c: slows a reaction and is used up
speeds up a reaction without being used up
items.e: Catalytic converters in cars use platinum.

c: The magnesium is being used up, so there are fewer collisions per second.
items.e: The rate falls as reactants are used up.

items.q: A flask on a balance loses 4 g of gas in 40 s (Harper's experiment). What is the average rate of mass loss?
Why is a 'disappearing cross' experiment repeated three times?
c: To check that the times are reliable and find an average.
items.e: Repeat trials.

items.q: Why do chlorine and sodium react so easily?
c: Sodium easily loses 1 electron and chlorine easily gains 1.
items.e: Outer electrons.

items.q: A gas is made by mixing acid with a metal. A burning splint pops. Which gas is it?
items.e: The pop test.

items.q: An iron nail turns reddish brown and flaky over weeks. What kind of change is this?
c: a physical change, because only the form changes
a chemical change, because new substances form
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: Water boils and turns to steam. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because new substances form
a physical change, because the substance stays the same
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: A sliced apple turns brown in air. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because new substances form
a physical change, because only the form changes
items.e: Evidence: gas, precipitate, colour change, light or temperature change from a reaction.

items.q: A student tests acid concentration but uses different temperatures in each trial. What is wrong?
c: Temperature is a second variable that also changes the rate.
items.e: Control variables.

items.q: Ice melts into water on the counter. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because new substances form
a physical change, because the substance stays the same
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: Why do doctors store some medicines in a refrigerator?
c: Cold slows the reactions that break the medicine down.
items.e: Lower rate.

items.q: Mia times how long a 1 cm magnesium ribbon takes to dissolve in acid at 20 °C, 30 °C and 40 °C. What is the dependent variable?
c: the time for the magnesium to dissolve
items.e: She measures the time.

items.q: Why do bakers in hot Australian summers keep dough in the fridge to slow its rising?
c: Lower temperature slows the reactions of yeast.
items.e: Temperature affects reaction rate.

items.q: Kai puts zinc, copper and magnesium strips into copper sulfate solution. Which metals will become coated with copper?
items.e: Only metals more reactive than copper displace it.

items.q: Ruby adds manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide. Bubbles of oxygen form quickly. After filtering, the manganese dioxide has the same mass. What is it?
items.e: Catalysts are not used up.

items.q: Why does a car's catalytic converter work better once the engine is warm?
c: Higher temperature makes the reactions on the catalyst faster.
items.e: Temperature and catalysts both raise rate.

items.q: Which observation is the best evidence that a new substance formed?
c: the liquid gets colder in a fridge
a solid precipitate appears when two clear solutions are mixed
items.e: Precipitate.

items.q: Noah heats green copper carbonate and it turns black, giving off a gas that turns limewater milky. Which type of reaction is this?
items.e: Copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide.

items.q: Dry ice turns directly into a gas. What kind of change is this?
c: a physical change, because the substance stays the same
a chemical change, because new substances form
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: Why do grain silos sometimes explode?
c: Fine grain dust has a huge surface area and burns very fast.
items.e: Surface area.

items.q: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine. What happens when chlorine gas is bubbled into potassium bromide solution?
c: Chlorine replaces bromine, so bromine forms.
items.e: More reactive halogen wins.

items.q: A student adds zinc to copper(II) sulfate. A red-brown solid forms and the blue colour fades. What happened?
c: Zinc replaced copper, so copper metal formed.
items.e: Displacement.
